# The Heat Is Unequal: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has become one of the defining challenges of urban life. Cities are inherently hotter than their surrounding countryside—the urban heat island effect can raise temperatures by several degrees, and in dense neighborhoods with abundant asphalt and little shade, the difference can be deadly. As heat waves grow longer, more frequent, and more intense, the question of how cities can remain livable in summer is no longer a matter of comfort but of survival. The good news is that urban heat is not a force of nature; it is a product of design choices, and different choices can undo much of the damage. The challenge is that every intervention carries tradeoffs, and those tradeoffs are rarely distributed evenly.

## Trees: The Oldest and Best Technology

The single most effective tool for cooling a city is also the oldest: shade. A mature street tree can lower the perceived temperature beneath its canopy by as much as 10 to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, not only by blocking the sun but through transpiration, the process by which leaves release water vapor.
